title: Mint Explainer: What makes a cloud sovereign?
title_bn: মিন্ট এক্সপ্লোরার: মেঘকে কি সার্বভৌম করে তোলে?
author: TechPulse
excerpt: As AI transforms computing infrastructure into a strategic asset, India is building a sovereign-cloud policy—raising the question of whether local data storage is enough without full control over physical hardware, encryption, and jurisdiction.
paragraph1: The case for sovereign cloud has become more compelling as cloud infrastructure has moved from an IT service to strategic infrastructure.SummaryAs AI transforms computing infrastructure into a strategic asset, India is building a sovereign-cloud policy—raising the question of whether local data storage is enough without full control over physical hardware, encryption, and jurisdiction.As the Indian government prepares to release a comprehensive consultation paper on AI regulation, data control and infrastructure ownership have emerged as critical priorities. With nations racing to build sovereign AI, true technological independence hinges on controlling the underlying cloud power, chips, and data centers that drive AI models. To address growing concerns over sensitive data and system access, MeitY has set up a committee to frame a sovereign-cloud policy. Mint explains what sovereign AI entails, why India needs a sovereign cloud, and whether domestic firms must build it.1. What does it mean for AI to be sovereign?AI sovereignty is often understood as a nation's ability to develop or control its own AI technology and models. But that is only part of the picture, as AI systems require data, computing power, and cloud infrastructure to train, operate, and scale. Access to computing power—particularly the GPUs required to train and run AI systems—and control over the supporting infrastructure are therefore strategically critical.For instance, if sensitive Indian data is processed on computing and cloud infrastructure controlled by a foreign entity, questions arise over who can access that data, who operates the systems, and which jurisdiction applies.
paragraph2: This makes controlling the cloud infrastructure where AI systems are trained and run a core element of AI sovereignty. Consequently, AI sovereignty cannot be viewed solely through the lens of AI models, technology, or tools. The underlying rails on which these systems run are just as important, if not more so, especially when handling government or other sensitive information.2. What makes a cloud sovereign?Simply locating servers in India does not make a cloud sovereign. To date, policy has focused primarily on data residency and localization. However, for a cloud to be truly considered sovereign, a country may need control over the physical infrastructure, the cloud technology and software control systems that manage it, operations and administration, encryption keys, and data access.There must also be explicit clarity on which country's laws govern the provider and its access to relevant data. These details are critical because a cloud platform can physically reside in India while its underlying technology or operational control remains with a foreign-headquartered firm governed by another nation's laws. India’s proposed framework will need to address these complex requirements, including how critical workloads can remain operational and controlled even during external disruptions.3.
paragraph3: Why does India want a sovereign cloud now?The case for a sovereign cloud has grown more compelling as cloud infrastructure has transitioned from an ordinary IT service to strategic national infrastructure, particularly with the rise of AI. Access to computing power, advanced chips, data, and the underlying infrastructure on which AI systems operate is increasingly a matter of national security and competitiveness.The US-China technology rivalry demonstrates how control over AI infrastructure can be weaponized as a geopolitical tool, as seen with US export controls restricting China's access to advanced chips. India's government has begun responding directly to these concerns. MeitY established the sovereign-cloud committee in August and held consultations with Google, AWS, and Apple in September. C-DAC has since issued an EoI for sovereign cloud services along with a tender for sovereign AI cloud and data-centre infrastructure, signaling that the government is transitioning from defining the regulatory framework to actively procuring the infrastructure.4. Can foreign cloud companies provide a sovereign cloud?Global cloud companies argue that sovereignty does not necessarily require domestic ownership. Microsoft, for instance, has positioned its new Hyderabad data-centre region, India South Central, as part of its “Sovereign Public Cloud” offering, featuring controls over data residency, encryption keys, and operational access.A Microsoft executive told Mint in a September interaction that Indian customers could obtain “full sovereign control” over their data, including where it resides, which data centres are used, and which laws apply.
paragraph4: AWS, too, provides digital-sovereignty controls and has partnered with Yotta to run sensitive government workloads inside NIC data centres using AWS services. Google offers similar sovereign-cloud capabilities, including dedicated and air-gapped infrastructure.The question for India, then, is whether these technical and operational controls are sufficient to meet its definition of sovereignty, or whether a sovereign cloud must also entail Indian ownership, control under Indian law and jurisdiction, or both.5. Does India need Indian cloud companies to build a sovereign cloud?This is ultimately a question of how India defines sovereignty. Indian ownership could provide the government with greater control over technology, infrastructure, and operations while reducing reliance on companies subject to foreign jurisdictions. Indian technology firms are already positioning themselves to provide sovereign cloud infrastructure for government and enterprise workloads.TCS, for instance, has developed SovereignSecure Cloud—an indigenous cloud tailored for government, public-sector, and regulated workloads—while Airtel’s Cloud offers control over the data, control plane, operations, and jurisdiction from within India. Yotta has likewise built sovereign AI infrastructure aimed at government and enterprise workloads.However, mandating an Indian provider could also mean forfeiting some of the scale, technology, and investment available from global hyperscalers. The central question, then, is whether India needs a domestic alternative to AWS, Microsoft, and Google, or whether it simply requires sufficient control over both foreign and domestic providers to ensure the cloud is sovereign.
paragraph5:
The path India chooses will determine whether it builds a parallel domestic cloud ecosystem or creates sovereignty standards that both global and Indian providers can meet.About the AuthorRadhika P NairRadhika P Nair is National Editor at Mint, bringing two decades of journalistic rigour to the newsroom. Since joining Mint in September 2025, she has specialised in crafting high-impact analytical narratives for Mint Long Story, focusing on startups, consumer brands, technology, the internet economy and travel.

A veteran of India’s digital evolution, Radhika has tracked the country’s startup ecosystem for over 15 years. She has reported on the rise of pioneers such as Flipkart, Zomato, Freshworks and Paytm from their nascent stages. Her career is defined by marquee reportage, including breaking the news of Flipkart’s historic $1-billion fundraise in 2014, then the largest by an Indian startup.

Before Mint, Radhika was Editorial Head at YourStory Media and contributed to leading publications including The Economic Times, NDTV Profit and Outlook Traveller. Her work is characterised by a human-focused, data-driven approach that seeks to understand shifting consumer behaviour with accuracy and depth. She is a two-time recipient of the Best Story of the Year award at The Economic Times. Notably, her Mint Long Story on Kochi’s water metro was cited in the 2026 Economic Survey of the Government of India.

Radhika holds a Master’s degree in Journalism, where she secured the first rank, and is a university gold medallist in Economics.
bangla_paragraph1: সেরকমই একটি তথ্য প্রযুক্তির পরিকাঠামো থেকে কৌশলগত পরিকাষ্ঠামীতে স্থানান্তরিত হওয়ার সাথে সাথে সার্বভৌম মেঘের ক্ষেত্রে আরও জোরদার হয়ে উঠেছে। সংক্ষিপ্তসারযেমন এআই কম্পিউটিং পরিকাঠে কৌশলগত সম্পদ রূপান্তর করে, ভারত একটি সার্বভারতীয় মেঘ নীতি তৈরি করছেভৌতিক হার্ডওয়্যার, এনক্রিপশন এবং বিচার বিভাগের উপর সম্পূর্ণ নিয়ন্ত্রণ ছাড়াই স্থানীয় ডেটা স্টোরেজ যথেষ্ট কিনা তা নিয়ে প্রশ্ন উত্থাপন করছে।যেমন ভারতীয় সরকার এআই নিয়ন্ত্রণের উপর একটি বিস্তৃত পরামর্শ পত্র প্রকাশের প্রস্তুতি নিচ্ছে, তথ্য নিয়ন্ত্রণ একটি
bangla_paragraph2: এটি ক্লাউড অবকাঠামো নিয়ন্ত্রণ করে যেখানে এআই সিস্টেমগুলি প্রশিক্ষিত এবং চালিত হয় এআই সার্বভৌমত্বের একটি মূল উপাদান। ফলস্বরূপ, এআই সের্বভৈমত্বকে কেবল এআই মডেল, প্রযুক্তি বা সরঞ্জামগুলির লেন্সের মাধ্যমে দেখা যায় না। এই সিস্টেমগুলির চালিত অন্তর্নিহিত রেলগুলি সমান গুরুত্বপূর্ণ, যদি না আরও বেশি হয়, বিশেষত সরকার বা অন্যান্য সংবেদনশীল তথ্য পরিচালনা করার সময়।
bangla_paragraph3: কেন ভারত এখন একটি সার্বভৌম মেঘ চায়?এখন একটি সারাবভৌমের জন্য মামলা আরও জোরালো হয়ে উঠেছে কারণ ক্লাউড অবকাঠামো একটি সাধারণ আইটি পরিষেবা থেকে কৌশলগত জাতীয় অবকাঁঠামোতে রূপান্তরিত হয়েছে, বিশেষত এআই-র উত্থানের সাথে। কম্পিউটিং শক্তি, উন্নত চিপ, ডেটা এবং ভিত্তিগত অবকাঙ্খার অ্যাক্সেস যা এআই সিস্টেমগুলি পরিচালনা করে তা ক্রমবর্ধমানভাবে জাতীয় সুরক্ষা এবং প্রতিযোগিতামূলকতার বিষয়। মার্কিন-চীন প্রযুক্তি প্রতিযোগিতা দেখায় যে কীভাবে এআই অবকাংখানের উপর নিয়ন্ত্রণ থাকতে পারে।
bangla_paragraph4: এডাব্লুএসও ডিজিটাল সার্বভৌমত্ব নিয়ন্ত্রণ সরবরাহ করে এবং এডব্লুএসের পরিষেবাগুলি ব্যবহার করে এনআইসি ডেটা সেন্টারের অভ্যন্তরে সংবেদনশীল সরকারী ওয়ার্কলোড চালানোর জন্য ইয়োটার সাথে অংশীদারিত্ব করেছে। গুগল ডেডিকেটেড এবং এয়ার-গ্যাপ ইনফ্রাস্ট্রাকচার সহ অনুরূপ সার্বভারতীয়-মেঘ ক্ষমতা সরবরাহ করে। ভারত, তারপরে প্রশ্নটি এই যে এই প্রযুক্তিগত এবং অপারেশনাল নিয়ন্ত্রণগুলি সার্বভাজনের সংজ্ঞা পূরণের জন্য পর্যাপ্ত কিনা, বা সার্বজনীন মেঘের সাথে ভারতীয় মালিকানা, নিয়ন্ত্রণ এবং ভারতীয় আইন এবং বিচার বিভাগের অধীনে নিয়ন্ত্রণও জড়িত থাকতে হবে কিনা।
bangla_paragraph5: ভারত যে পথ বেছে নেবে তা নির্ধারণ করবে যে এটি একটি সমান্তরাল দেশীয় ক্লাউড বাস্তুতন্ত্র তৈরি করে কিনা বা সার্বভৌমত্বের মান তৈরি করে যা বিশ্ব এবং ভারতীয় উভয় সরবরাহকারী পূরণ করতে পারে।লেখক সম্পর্কেরাধিকা পি নায়ারমিন্টের জাতীয় সম্পাদক, নিউজরুমে দুই দশকের সাংবাদিকতার কঠোরতা নিয়ে আসেন। সেপ্টেম্বর ২০২৫ সালে মিন্ট যোগদানের পর থেকে তিনি স্টার্টআপস, ভোক্তা ব্র্যান্ড, প্রযুক্তি, ইন্টারনেট ইকোনোমির উপর দৃষ্টি নিবদ্ধ করে মিনট লং স্টোরির জন্য উচ্চ-প্রভাব বিশ্লেষণাত্মক বিবরণ তৈরিতে বিশেষীকরণ করেছেন।

title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
title_bn: কিভাবে একজন হ্যাকার এআই এজেন্ট এবং কয়েক হাজার ডলার ব্যবহার করে অনেকগুলো সাইটে ঢুকেছিল
author: TechPulse
excerpt: AI-CYBERCRIME/ (PIX):EXCLUSIVE-How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
paragraph1: * Report finds AI agents attempted 1,200 break-ins and compromised more than 100 sites* Reuters identified victims including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins by reviewing hacker's activity* Chinese-speaking hacker was one of several discovered by cybersecurity researcherBy Raphael SatterWASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, home appliance company SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins .Yet the hacker did almost none of the work.The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence, tasking AI agents with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge.In a report provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Monday, Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, Fagerland said he found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world.Fagerland's report on the Chinese-speaking hacker did not name the victims, but Reuters was able to establish the victims' identities by independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity.At a time of rising anxiety over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor."It's a new world now," said Fagerland.
paragraph2: Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorized extraction of data.Deere told Reuters it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors."Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages.FEW INSTRUCTIONS, MANY HACKSOne of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange.
paragraph3: The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on September 25, they set their AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites.Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly $5,000 worth of tokens, or about $50 per successful hack.Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — said he was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims. In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after hours of trial and error, reported leveraging it to trick the server into executing malicious commands."
paragraph4: It's not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff."Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions. In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not my intention."NO SUPERVISION NEEDEDThe ability of agentic AI systems to autonomously discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world. Rogue agents inadvertently unleashed by major AI companies have hacked their way out of computer labs,broken into government websites, and engaged in unsanctioned social engineering attempts. South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by a series of well-publicized hacks attributed to AI-using cybercriminals.
paragraph5: AI agents are increasingly becoming staples of the cybercriminal underground. In August, the Israeli firm Gambit Security found that Russian-speaking extortionists had leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool to break into seven organizations. In September, Gambit documented an AI agent-driven spree that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records. Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said that discussions about how to use autonomous agents were surging across cybercriminal forums.Fagerland said he had previously assumed hacker-agents would need at least some supervision. He said it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that."The development in this field is astounding," he said.

title: MeitY Asks Meta To Review Content Recommendation Algorithms
title_bn: মেটওয়াই মেটাকে কনটেন্ট রেফারেন্স অ্যালগরিদম পর্যালোচনা করতে বলেছে
author: TechPulse
excerpt: The Centre has asked Meta, which operates Instagram and Facebook, to review its recommendation algorithms to prevent disproportionate exposure to…
paragraph1: SUMMARYMeitY has asked Meta to review its recommendation algorithms to prevent disproportionate exposure to a limited set of narratives and the amplification of potentially misleading content The advisory seeks changes to how Facebook and Instagram recommend content, drawing criticism from digital rights advocate Apar Gupta over its legal basis and implications for lawful expression Meta has been asked to strengthen content review mechanisms, provide context for material depicting public events, and report the measures taken with immediate effect The Centre has asked Meta, which operates Instagram and Facebook, to review its recommendation algorithms to prevent disproportionate exposure to a limited set of narratives and strengthen checks on content that could cause public disorder or incite violence. In an advisory dated October 10, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) directed Meta to provide adequate context for photographs, videos, graphics and other content depicting ongoing public events, particularly when their authenticity, date, location or circumstances may not be readily apparent to users, according to PTI. The advisory also called for a review of Meta’s recommendation and content-ranking mechanisms to prevent potentially misleading, manipulated or out-of-context material from being disproportionately amplified or repeatedly recommended to users. “Ensure that recommendation systems do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives, and endeavour to provide appropriate diversity of relevant and credible information,” the advisory said. It also called for stronger mechanisms to rapidly identify, review and escalate content that gains significant reach through recommendation systems and could potentially cause widespread public confusion, apprehension, violence, or disturbances to public order.
paragraph2: The advisory came amid protests in Delhi by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Similar concerns over content moderation were raised by the government earlier, following a CJP protest at Jantar Mantar in June. While the advisory does not specify what prompted the government’s move, IT Ministry sources told PTI that agencies had flagged concerns over Meta’s recommendation algorithms, which allegedly appeared to favour certain types of content over others. What MeitY Wants Meta To Change The advisory asked Meta to provide users with a diversity of relevant and credible information through its recommendation systems. It flagged videos, images, statements and graphics relating to public events that were being “prominently displayed and recommended to users” across Meta’s platforms.
paragraph3: It warned that such material, when circulated without adequate context or amplified disproportionately, “may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity”. MeitY asked the company to pay particular attention to old or selectively edited visuals presented as current events, unverified claims about emergencies and police action, and audio-visual material relating to law-and-order situations that lack adequate context. It also called for stronger mechanisms to identify and review content that could incite violence or other unlawful activity. The advisory invoked the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the IT Rules, 2021, which require intermediaries to exercise due diligence and inform users about prohibited content. It also called for timely cooperation with law enforcement agencies and other authorised government bodies.
paragraph4: Meta was asked to implement the measures “with immediate effect” and inform the ministry of the action taken. The advisory stated that any action must comply with applicable laws while respecting lawful expression and legitimate public discourse. The directions have drawn criticism from digital rights advocates over its potential implications for freedom of expression and content moderation. Apar Gupta, founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation, described it as a “continuing censorship directive”, arguing that it was not legally binding. Gupta urged MeitY to withdraw the advisory and called on Meta to publicly disclose every takedown and instance of downranking carried out in response to it.
paragraph5: He also questioned the legal basis for the directive, arguing that phrases such as content circulated “without adequate context” and periods of “heightened public-order sensitivity” were not tied to specific provisions of the IT Act or the IT Rules.
bangla_paragraph1: সংক্ষিপ্তসারMeitY মেটাকে তার সুপারিশ অ্যালগরিদমগুলি পর্যালোচনা করতে বলেছে যাতে সীমিত সংখ্যক বিবরণ এবং সম্ভাব্য বিভ্রান্তিকর বিষয়বস্তুর বিস্তার প্রতিরোধ করা যায়। এই উপদেশটি ফেসবুক এবং ইনস্টাগ্রাম কীভাবে সামগ্রী প্রস্তাব করে তাতে পরিবর্তন আনতে চায়।
bangla_paragraph2: নির্বাচনী তালিকার বিশেষ নিবিড় সংশোধন (এসআইআর) নিয়ে দিল্লিতে প্রধান নির্বাচন কমিশনার জ্ঞানেশ কুমারের পদত্যাগের দাবিতে কোকড়া জনতা পার্টি (সিজেপি) এবং বিরোধী দলগুলির প্রতিবাদের মধ্যে এই পরামর্শ এসেছে। জুন মাসে জন্তর মন্টরে সিজেপি প্রতিবাদ করার পরে, সামগ্রী সংযম সম্পর্কে সরকার আগেও অনুরূপ উদ্বেগ উত্থাপন করেছিল। যদিও পরামর্শটি সরকারকে এই পদক্ষেপের জন্য কী বলেছিল তা নির্দিষ্ট করে না, আইটি মন্ত্রকের সূত্র পিটিআইকে জানিয়েছে যে সংস্থাগুলি উদ্বেগ প্রকাশ করেছিল।
bangla_paragraph3: এটি সতর্ক করে দিয়েছিল যে, এই ধরনের সামগ্রী, যখন পর্যাপ্ত প্রসঙ্গে বা অপ্রয়োজনীয়ভাবে প্রসারিত হয়, তখন জনসাধারণের বিভ্রান্তি, উদ্বেগ এবং জনশৃঙ্খলা এবং সামাজিক প্রশান্তির ব্যাঘাতের দিকে অবদান রাখতে পারে। MeitY কোম্পানিকে বর্তমান ঘটনা হিসাবে উপস্থাপিত পুরানো বা নির্বাচনীভাবে সম্পাদিত ভিজ্যুয়ালগুলিতে বিশেষ মনোযোগ দিতে বলেছিল, জরুরী অবস্থা এবং পুলিশ কর্ম সম্পর্কে যাচাই করা দাবি এবং আইন-শৃংখলা পরিস্থিতি সম্পর্কিত অডিও-ভিজ্যুয়েল সামগ্রী যা পর্যাপ্ত প্রেক্ষাপটে নেই। এটি আরও জোরদার করার আহ্বান জানিয়েছে
bangla_paragraph4: মেটাকে ব্যবস্থাগুলি তাত্ক্ষণিকভাবে কার্যকর করতে বলা হয়েছিল এবং গৃহীত পদক্ষেপ সম্পর্কে মন্ত্রককে অবহিত করতে বলা হয়েছে। উপদেষ্টা বিবৃতিতে বলা হয়েছে যে আইনী মত প্রকাশ এবং বৈধ জনমতকে সম্মান জানিয়ে যে কোনও পদক্ষেপ প্রযোজ্য আইন মেনে চলতে হবে। নির্দেশাবলীটি মত প্রকাশের স্বাধীনতা এবং সামগ্রী মডারেশনের সম্ভাব্য প্রভাবের জন্য ডিজিটাল অধিকার সমর্থকদের সমালোচনা করেছে। ইন্টারনেট ফ্রিডম ফাউন্ডেশনের প্রতিষ্ঠাতা-পরিচালক আপার গুপ্ত এটিকে  অব্যাহত সেন্সরশিপ  হিসাবে বর্ণনা করেছেন।
bangla_paragraph5: তিনি আরও বলেন, 'যদিও এই নির্দেশিকাটি আইনী ভিত্তিতে প্রয়োগ করা হয়, তবে এটি আইটি আইন বা আইটি বিধিমালার নির্দিষ্ট বিধানের সাথে যুক্ত নয়।

paragraph2: This translates to an oversubscription of 101.78X. paragraph3: 67X. The qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) have placed bids for 7.38 Cr shares against the 24.32 Lakh shares reserved for them, translating into an oversubscription of 30.37X. It was bought out in 2012 by promoters and cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza. Since then, the company has pivoted to design and development of advanced imaging and sensor systems used for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting, and other military applications.

In Q1 FY27, the company reported operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr.

title: Barcelona-based Enzo Ventures closes €20M Fund II backing Southern European founders
title_bn: Barcelona-based Enzo Ventures closes €20M Fund II backing Southern European founders
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Barcelona-based Enzo Ventures has closed its second fund, a €20m fund which is backing Southern European founders at the pre-seed stage.Fund II follows Enzo’s strategy it began in 2023, when it invest...
paragraph1: Barcelona-based Enzo Ventures has closed its second fund, a €20m fund which is backing Southern European founders at the pre-seed stage. Fund II follows Enzo’s strategy it began in 2023, when it invested in its first fund, which backed Southern European founders and diaspora entrepreneurs at the very start of their journey. Enzo says Fund II has been designed around a simple principle: keep doing what worked in Fund I, a €10m fund, but with more capital and a stronger platform behind it. Enzo defines diaspora entrepreneurs as those founders leaving cities like Barcelona and Lisbon to build companies in cities like London and Paris, while maintaining deep ties to the talent networks and entrepreneurial communities they came from.
paragraph2: The firm is looking to identify these founders before the broader VC market. The new fund is deploying cheques of between €250,000 and €600,000. The new fund has already invested in three startups: London-based Cori Clinical and investments in startups in Madrid and Zurich. Enzo’s portfolio includes Orbio and Murphy, which Enzo says are now generating millions of euros in revenue.
paragraph3: Enzo was founded by Edgar Vicente and Iván Fernández Lucas, who both have a background in startups. Vicente was just 23 when he co-founded Enzo. The pair launched Enzo to address what they saw as a gap in Southern Europe: early-stage capital that is founder-friendly, globally ambitious, and willing to take “day-zero” risk. They believed many local VCs were overly conservative.
paragraph4: Vicente, founding partner, Enzo Ventures, said: “When we started investing in 2023, our conviction was that something structural was changing in Southern Europe. “The new generation of founders coming out of the region was more ambitious, more technical and much more global from day one. We didn't want to build a fund around where companies were incorporated. We wanted to build one around where exceptional founders came from.

title: Even Healthcare Raises $50 Mn To Expand Hospital Network Across Bengaluru
title_bn: Even Healthcare Raises $50 Mn To Expand Hospital Network Across Bengaluru
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Bengaluru-based managed care startup Even Healthcare has raised $50 Mn (about ₹475 Cr) in a Series B funding round led…
paragraph1: SUMMARYEven Healthcare has raised $50 Mn in a Series B round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures, with participation from Alpha Wave The funding will support the managed care startup’s hospital expansion in Bengaluru as it scales back its insurance business Even plans to add four hospitals by the end of FY27 to its existing network of two facilities before expanding to other cities Bengaluru-based managed care startup Even Healthcare has raised $50 Mn (about ₹475 Cr) in a Series B funding round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures, with participation from Alpha Wave. The all-equity primary round takes its total funding to over $120 Mn, the startup said in a statement. Even will use the proceeds primarily to expand its hospital network in Bengaluru. It plans to open another hospital by the end of 2026, followed by three more by the end of FY27. It currently operates two multispeciality hospitals on Race Course Road and in HBR Layout.
paragraph2: The startup plans to enter other cities after strengthening its Bengaluru presence. “We want to make sure that Bengaluru patients and members are pretty well served,” cofounder Mayank Banerjee told Inc42. Even said its valuation had tripled since its previous fundraise 18 months ago, without disclosing its latest valuation. The startup last raised $20 Mn earlier this year to expand its hospital network and launch new facilities. Founded in 2020 by Banerjee, Matilde Giglio, and Alessandro Ialongo, Even offers an integrated managed care model combining preventive care, outpatient consultations, diagnostics, insurance access, hospitalisation, and post-discharge recovery.
paragraph3: The startup aims to reduce healthcare costs by managing patients’ health beyond individual hospital visits. Its services include telemedicine, at-home blood tests, and medical guidance, alongside cashless hospitalisation through insurance partners. Even employs salaried doctors whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed or revenue generated. The startup said it assesses doctors on patient outcomes, recovery timelines, and re-admissions. Banerjee said around 85-90% of Even members living near one of its Bengaluru hospitals choose the startup for their healthcare needs.
paragraph4: Even also uses an AI-based quality system to review cases against clinical protocols in real time. It recently launched Even Spotlight, a dashboard tracking clinical outcomes and patient-reported metrics. The startup said unplanned re-admissions in programmes run with insurance partners remained below 1%, compared with an industry range of 8-15%. It also claimed average hospital stays were 40% shorter, while proactive care helped more than 200 members avoid hospitalisation, saving an estimated ₹15 Cr to ₹16 Cr. Even claims to serve more than 2.
paragraph5: 5 Lakh members across 10 cities, having tripled its membership over the past year. The hospital expansion follows reports in August that Even laid off around 350 employees as it scaled down its insurance business and shifted resources towards a hospital-led healthcare model. The cuts affected 30-35% of its workforce across multiple teams.

title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
title_bn: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Even Healthcare reaches a $300 million valuation in a Khosla Ventures-led round as it plans to expand its hospital network in India.
paragraph1: Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded. The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million. Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills. That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs. Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services. “The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.
paragraph2: Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary. “We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch. Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment. Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes. The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even.
paragraph3: The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills. Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison. Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).
paragraph4: Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said. Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show. In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup-news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting. Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time.
paragraph5: The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable. “Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said. title: AI agents are only as good as the personal information you share. That raises privacy concerns
title_bn: AI agents are only as good as the personal information you share. That raises privacy concerns
author: TechPulse
excerpt: AI agents are only as good as the personal information you share. That raises privacy concerns
paragraph1: Matt Robb wanted to sell his computer keyboard.So he made a listing on Facebook Marketplace — and, as an experiment late last month, he put Meta's new artificial intelligence agent Muse in the driver's seat.“I kind of went into it like a guinea pig,” said Robb, a Toronto-based content creator who regularly reviews consumer tech. He had seen Muse's plush toy-looking avatar pop up on Instagram and decided to see if the AI agent could spare him some online bargaining.Muse got to work. But within a day, Robb got an alarming update: A buyer he didn't know had shown up outside his house late at night. How? Muse had struck a deal on its own and shared Robb's home address after agreeing to a pickup. It even sent an automated “Yep, I'm here!” message from his account when the buyer arrived — all without Robb's knowledge.“Not only did it give my address when the guy asked and it accepted the offer, but it literally was almost like teasing the guy (about me being there when I wasn't),” said Robb, who also detailed the experience in his now widely-shared social media posts. “That really baffled me.”Many have welcomed AI agents into their online lives, and raved about how personalized assistants like Muse can handle everyday tasks with ease — from snagging a dinner reservation or planning a trip, to organizing email inboxes.
paragraph2: But like other AI bots, the agents are only as good as the information they have access to. They perform better the more they know about a user — and perhaps also that person’s friends, family and even colleagues. That raises privacy concerns.Robb and the buyer eventually made amends, and Meta reached out to talk through what went wrong. But the episode showed real-world risks that can arise from sharing extensive personal information with the technology.“Using an AI agent is similar to handing someone your keys and a to-do list,” said Veronica Rivera, assistant professor at Georgia Tech’s School of Cybersecurity and Privacy. “How helpful they are, and by extension how risky, depends on which keys you hand over.”Since its September launch, downloads of Meta's Muse app have skyrocketed. And competition is only growing. OpenAI recently rolled out its own lineup of “always on” AI helpers, called dots, which can be integrated into ChatGPT and workplace platforms like Slack and Microsoft Teams.Older generative AI chatbots, like the standard version of ChatGPT, respond to specific prompts. At the user's request, they can write essays, generate new images or music, or even write lines of code.Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots go a step further to perform day-to-day tasks on a person's behalf.
paragraph3: AI agents are powered by the same large language models as chatbots, but they run in a loop. That allows an agent to take proactive steps, even when the user isn't looking.“One of the things that makes these AI agents really appealing is that they are unprecedentedly useful,” said Rivera, who is also a Microsoft-funded Computing Research Association Trustworthy AI Research Fellow.But the convenience comes with the price of sharing more details about your life.Once AI agents obtain users' information, it's very difficult to fully withdraw access, said Ebrahim Bagheri, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information.“If you provide access to your credit card to an agent, the agent now immediately has access to all of the historical transactions … they will immediately — within less than seconds — ingest all of that data,” Bagheri said. And while users can later withdraw access, Bagheri said there's “no taking back” data the agent has already seen, and how developers store historical data can be murky.Both Meta and OpenAI outline privacy policies for their new AI agents, which operate on their own dedicated cloud computers. You can turn off memory sharing between dots and ChatGPT, but information the agent previously received isn't automatically deleted. OpenAI gives users an option to request access to, delete or correct personal information, although rights can vary depending on where you live.Meta's Muse gives users options to delete message history and other information, too. For day-to-day use, the agent prompts users for access permissions — and Meta has said Muse learns about a user and who they interact with “based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share.” But the company says that all stays secure for each user.
paragraph4: But the tech giant also notes that Muse can still “make mistakes or take unexpected actions.”In Robb's case, he learned the disclosure of his address came down to “always allow” permissions he granted when he first let Muse on his Facebook Marketplace profile, where he had shared his pickup address. But he warned others could similarly misunderstand the extent of that access — and said he initially thought the AI agent would check with him before sharing that information or accepting offers, regardless.His AI agent didn’t follow the rest of his instructions without error, either. For another item Robb was selling, Muse seemingly suggested he would accept a price $100 below the previously-set minimum. When reached by The Associated Press, Meta acknowledged the agent's error without offering further comment.Robb later largely disconnected Muse from his apps. In an interview earlier this month, he said it could've been a far worse situation, especially “if some stranger turned up to someone more vulnerable's house.” Still, Robb said he expects these agents to be fine-tuned and he would consider re-enabling Muse in the future. He's since been testing another AI agent — Grok Bot from Elon Musk's X, which launched in beta in August.Other tech companies have become wary of the influx of AI agents. Earlier this month, Apple said it would introduce new controls for its Mac operating system in response to AI agents' broader access of apps like mail, messages and even browsing history without users’ “full knowledge and understanding.”“As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially,” Apple wrote in an Oct.
paragraph5: 2 update.Apple didn’t specify any developers or agents by name, but the update arrived after Inc. Magazine columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse watched notifications on his Mac — including Messages — without him giving the agent that specific access.Meta spokesperson Andy Stone has maintained such integration is “entirely opt-in,” writing on social media last month that users would have to enable both the Apple security feature “Full Disk Access” and a Messages connector through Muse. Aten said he didn’t grant the agent those permissions.Even those who do not join the AI agent boom aren’t necessarily shielded. Consumers who don’t download an AI agent might still interact with others who do. And beyond potential confusion when AI sends messages on behalf of a user, experts warn of ripple effects when it comes to privacy.“When your agent reads your inbox or your texts, it’s also reading what your friends and family sent you, even if they never explicitly agreed to that,” Rivera said.

excerpt: Apple has redesigned Dynamic Island for the iPhone 18 Pro, shrinking its cutout while retaining Face ID and expanding support from two to three simultaneous Live Activities.
paragraph1: Apple has redesigned Dynamic Island for the iPhone 18 Pro, shrinking its cutout while retaining Face ID and expanding support from two to three simultaneous Live Activities. Apple’s Dynamic Island: How does it work on iPhone 18 Pro and foldable Duo? Explained(Representative AI image)Apple’s Dynamic Island is a pill-shaped area at the top of the iPhone screen. It replaces the notch and shows alerts, app notifications, and updates from ongoing tasks. You can tap or hold it to see details and use controls.The feature was launched on the iPhone 14 Pro in 2022. It has been available on every subsequent Pro model, as well as the full iPhone 15 and 16 series (and later). However, it works differently on the iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone Duo.Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 ProDynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro combines a smaller cutout with support for more simultaneous Live Activities. It shows updates from ongoing activities while keeping their details accessible. The changes cover both the hardware and the software surrounding it.On the hardware side, the cutout is smaller and narrower than on previous models. Apple achieved this by moving the Face ID infrared camera under the display.
paragraph2: There is a specialised pixel arrangement that lets infrared light pass through.This leaves more usable screen area on the Pro model’s 6.3-inch display while still supporting full Face ID functionality. It supports unlocking and Apple Pay, and app authentication continues to work as before.The software upgrade allows up to three Live Activities at once. These are ongoing updates from tasks running in the background. For example, Dynamic Island can show an Uber ride, a sports score and a kitchen timer together. A workout session is another activity it can display.Earlier versions showed one main activity in the cutout alongside a second, separate bubble (a maximum of two). The revised layout uses the narrower cutout and surrounding space for three activities. This helps users follow several tasks from the same area.To focus on an activity, tap its indicator. On models that support three activities, you can also swipe across Dynamic Island to move between them.
paragraph3: For more information, touch and hold the activity you want to view.This opens a larger notification card containing further details. Swipe up to collapse the card into its compact position again.These changes give users more screen space and easier access to several ongoing updates at once. The hardware keeps the necessary sensors within a smaller area, while the software arranges up to three activities around that space and provides simple touch controls.Dynamic Island on iPhone DuoThe iPhone Duo has two displays. Each display has its own front camera. The outer camera sits in the corner. It is always visible. The inner camera stays hidden behind the screen until it is active.On the outer display, the camera area expands into the Dynamic Island. It appears when a Live Activity runs. The island sits atop a vertical column on the side of the screen.
paragraph4:
The status bar, toolbar and tab bar sit below it. Apple says these controls move to the side to save vertical space for content.The controls stay on the side when the phone opens in landscape. This keeps the experience consistent across both displays. The exception is the inner display in portrait mode. It has enough vertical space to keep standard horizontal bars.About the AuthorSounak MukhopadhyaySounak Mukhopadhyay covers trending news, sports and entertainment for LiveMint. His reporting focuses on fast-moving stories, box office performance, digital culture and major cricket developments. He combines real-time updates with clear context for everyday readers.

Sounak brings newsroom experience across breaking news, explainers and long-form features. He has a strong emphasis on accuracy, verification and responsible storytelling. His work tracks audience behaviour, celebrity influence and the business of sport and cinema. He helps readers understand why a story matters beyond the headline.
paragraph5:
Sounak has contributed to widely read digital publications. He continues to build a body of journalism shaped by consistency, speed and editorial clarity. He is particularly interested in the intersection of media, popular culture and public conversation in contemporary India.

At LiveMint, he writes daily coverage as well as analytical pieces that interpret numbers, trends and cultural moments in accessible language. His approach prioritises factual depth, balanced framing and reader trust. The reporting aligns with modern newsroom standards of transparency and credibility.

Outside daily reporting, he explores storytelling across formats including podcasts, filmmaking and narrative non-fiction. Through his journalism, Sounak aims to document the rhythms of modern entertainment and sports while maintaining rigorous editorial integrity.

Sounak continues to develop audience-focused journalism that connects speed with substance in a rapidly-changing information environment. His work seeks clarity, trust and lasting public value in every story he reports.

title: Urban Company Slumps 9.5% After Q2 Loss Widens, Board Clears ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise
title_bn: Urban Company Slumps 9.5% After Q2 Loss Widens, Board Clears ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Shares of home services company Urban Company slumped 9.5% to ₹143.30 apiece on the BSE during early trading today, following…
paragraph1: SUMMARYUrban Company shares slumped 9.5% to ₹143.30 on the BSE after its Q2 FY27 loss widened and the board approved a fundraise of up to ₹2,500 Cr InstaHelp’s losses have constrained the company’s financial flexibility as it pursues growth opportunities, including Native’s planned entry into residential air conditioners Net loss widened to ₹182.5 Cr from ₹59.3 Cr a year earlier, while operating revenue rose 41% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr. Shares of home services company Urban Company slumped 9.
paragraph2: 5% to ₹143.30 apiece on the BSE during early trading today, following its Q2 FY27 results and board approval for a fundraise of up to ₹2,500 Cr. At 12:10 IST, the stock was trading 8.56% lower at ₹144.75 on the BSE. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹22,323 Cr (about $2.7 Bn) at the time.
paragraph3: Urban Company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹182.5 Cr for Q2 FY27 on Friday (October 16) as against a loss of ₹59.3 Cr a year earlier and ₹92.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue rose 41% to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, total expenses increased 61.
paragraph4: 5% to ₹745.7 Cr, driven largely by higher spending on its quick household help business, InstaHelp. The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr, including what it described as a “deliberate” ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding the vertical, adjusted EBITDA stood at ₹30 Cr. The company’s board also approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr through equity shares and/or convertible securities via preferential allotment or private placement. Urban Company said the proceeds would strengthen InstaHelp’s market leadership, support investment across its three businesses, and fund potential acquisitions. It is also exploring entry into the residential air conditioner market under its consumer appliances brand ‘Native’, which currently sells water purifiers and smart locks.
paragraph5: Management said it could meet its profitability targets without additional capital, although InstaHelp’s losses limited its financial flexibility. Despite the rise in its loss, Emkay Global Financial Services maintained its ‘Buy’ rating for Urban Company and raised its target price to ₹200 from ₹190, citing growth opportunities across its segments and the strength of its core business. The brokerage highlighted low penetration of its core services, expansion into Tier II cities, improving international profitability, and the Saudi Arabia business’ progress towards breakeven. It also identified Native as a growth opportunity and said InstaHelp was driving higher customer engagement.

title: UC Eyes More Capital, Burma Burma’s IPO & More
title_bn: UC Eyes More Capital, Burma Burma’s IPO & More
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Inside UC’s ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise Plan A year after listing, Urban Company is back in the market for more funds.…
paragraph1: Inside UC’s ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise Plan A year after listing, Urban Company is back in the market for more funds. The company plans to raise ₹2,500 Cr as it chases profitability, eyes new businesses and fights a costly battle for home services supremacy. Will the fresh capital fortify UC’s competitive posture? A Bigger War Chest: Urban Company’s board has approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr through equity or convertible securities. While it is yet to decide on the route for the fundraise, the management believes that the proceeds would absorb short-term operational burn without constraining internal cash flows. The ₹2,500 Cr Buffer: While the company maintains that it can reach EBITDA breakeven by FY28 without fresh capital, the fundraise provides balance sheet flexibility. Simultaneously, the capital buffer will also enable UC to fund new products, execute new acquisitions and expand internationally without compromising its core margins. The InstaHelp Drag: The timing is significant. The company’s net loss more than tripled YoY to ₹182.5 Cr in Q2 FY27. Largely to blame for this was the loss from its quick service vertical, InstaHelp, and continued investments in the business. What has not helped is the intensifying competition from Snabbit and Pronto, which is forcing UC to spend heavily on user acquisition, retaining gig workers and market expansion. The Native Expansion: Parallely, UC is also foraying into the residential AC market under its Native brand. The new venture will rely solely on the UC app for distribution, focusing its initial years on product feedback and calibrated capital allocation. While service demand does not automatically translate into appliance sales, the company will be banking on its years of data on consumer pain points and product gaps to carve its niche. With InstaHelp consuming cash and Native entering a new category, can Urban Company use the potential ₹2,500 Cr war chest to enter and dominate Indian homes? Let’s find out… From The Editor’s Desk 🥗 Burma Burma All Set For IPO The restaurant chain’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Pvt Ltd, has filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale component of up to 2.
paragraph2: 8 Cr shares. Founded in 2013, Hunger Pangs operates Burma Burma, which serves vegetarian Burmese cuisine. It operates 22 restaurants across nine cities. The startup also plans to open Japanese restaurants and noodle shops under a new brand. On the financial front, the company saw its operating revenue zoom 46.6% YoY to ₹155.5 Cr in FY26, while net loss widened nearly 31X YoY to ₹15.4 Cr. Hunger Pangs also reported a top line of ₹53.7 Cr against a profit of ₹1.1 Cr in Q1 FY27. ✈️ ixigo’s Q2 Snapshot The travel tech major reported a net profit of ₹63.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 against a loss of ₹3.5 Cr in the year ago quarter. The OTA swung to the black on the back of a one-time gain, improving margins and operating revenue rising nearly 13% YoY to ₹321 Cr. Train remained ixigo’s largest revenue-generating segment, with GTV rising to ₹2,256 Cr during the quarter. The flight GTV also rose 37% YoY to ₹2,184.
paragraph3: 3 Cr, while bus booking generated a GTV of ₹752.7 Cr. Going forward, the listed OTA plans to continue investing in hotels and AI as “key drivers” of its long-term growth. At the end of September 2026, ixigo’s hotel inventory covered more than 70,000 properties across 1,100 towns. 📈 Startup Funding Rebounds Indian new-age tech ventures cumulatively bagged $236.2 Mn last week, up 92% from $123 Mn in the preceding week. Deal count, however, stayed at 25. Boldfit and GreenCell Mobility took the biggest cheques home at $42 Mn and $35 Mn, respectively. AI startups dominated the funding charts last week and lapped up $53.4 Mn across six deals. Following suit was ecommerce, which emerged as the second-most funded sector and secured $48.3 Mn. Early-stage funding activity remained strong as pre-seed and seed-stage startups raised $25.9 Mn across 11 deals last week. Meanwhile, Accel emerged as the most active investor last week and backed four startups. 📊 Mixed Week For Startup Stocks Of the 67 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage, 31 gained between 0.03% and 17.
paragraph4: 63% last week. The remaining 36 declined by as much as 18.43%. AceVector and Tracxn emerged as the biggest losers, while Yudiz and Nazara gained the most. The combined market capitalisation of the 67 new-age tech companies rose 3.8% to $160.6 at the end of last week, up from $154.71 Bn in the preceding week. Investors will track September infrastructure output, PMI readings and RBI monetary policy committee meeting for market cues this week. Inflationary pressures, crude oil prices and foreign investor flows will also decide market direction. 🚚 Ekart Mixed FY26 Show Instakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in FY26. The company managed to narrow its losses by 98.3% YoY to ₹26 Cr in the fiscal under review compared to ₹1,508 Cr in FY25. The losses declined despite Ekart’s top line falling 4.2% YoY to ₹13,194 Cr in FY26. Of this, Flipkart itself contributed ₹9,112 Cr, or about 69% of the total operating revenue. Meanwhile, expenses stood at ₹13,638 Cr in FY26, albeit down 13% YoY.
paragraph5: Founded in 2009, Ekart offers fulfillment services not only for Flipkart and Myntra but also for external D2C brands, online sellers and retailers. The logistics platform claims to operate 70 fulfilment centres, 80 sortation facilities and 3500 delivery hubs across India. Inc42 Markets RECOMMENDED FOR yOU Inc42 Startup Spotlight How EdgeVerse Is Helping Two-Wheelers Spot Danger India is home to one of the largest two-wheeler markets in the world. Yet, collision-prevention systems remain largely limited to cars. Enter EdgeVerse, a startup building an AI-powered stack to bring advanced rider assistance features to two-wheelers. ADAS For Bikes: Founded in 2023, EdgeVerse is developing Perceiva, an advanced rider assistance system (ARAS), for two-wheelers. Akin to ADAS for cars, the system combines camera, radar and GPS inputs to deliver real-time perception and safety for two-wheelers. EdgeVerse’s Tech Stack: The startup’s hardware platform is designed to run perception workloads at the edge, reducing dependence on cloud connectivity. The startup also claims that its technology can work with existing camera and radar architectures, enabling OEMs to add safety intelligence without significantly increasing vehicle cost or hardware complexity. The Road Ahead: Having already conducted road testing, EdgeVerse now plans to enter the market through OEM partnerships in late-2026. It has also set its eyes on experimenting with use cases like industrial automation and other edge-AI applications. Going forward, the startup plans to accelerate the development and commercialisation of its perception technology. With the Indian ADAS market projected to become a $3.1 Bn opportunity by 2031, can EdgeVerse make rider safety a standard feature on India’s two-wheelers? title: The Pant Project Raises ₹109 Cr To Expand Store Network & Portfolio
title_bn: The Pant Project Raises ₹109 Cr To Expand Store Network & Portfolio
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Menswear brand The Pant Project has raised ₹109 Cr (about $11.5 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by…
paragraph1: SUMMARYThe Pant Project has raised ₹109 Cr in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), with participation from existing investor Sorin Investments The funding will support the bottomwear specialist’s push to build a broader menswear business, with a focus on jeans, athleisure, and casualwear The startup plans to expand its store network from 25 to 150 over the next two to three years and has separately secured venture debt from Alteria Capital for an undisclosed amount Menswear brand The Pant Project has raised ₹109 Cr (about $11.5 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India) to expand its offline presence and broaden its apparel portfolio. Existing investor Sorin Investments also participated in the round, alongside family offices and angel investors, including Anisha Saraf, B&K Securities, MGA Ventures, and B2V Ventures. The latest round takes the startup’s total funding to over $15.75 Mn. It previously raised $4.
paragraph2: 25 Mn in a Series A round led by Sorin Investments in 2024, following four years of bootstrapping. Separately, The Pant Project secured venture debt financing from Alteria Capital for an undisclosed amount. The startup plans to increase its exclusive brand store network from 25 to 150 over the next two to three years. It will also deploy the fresh capital to broaden its menswear portfolio, with a focus on jeans, athleisure, and casualwear. title: Will The Jio Platforms IPO Live Up To Its Billing?
title_bn: Will The Jio Platforms IPO Live Up To Its Billing?
author: TechPulse
excerpt: It’s already called the biggest IPO in India, but Reliance Industries Limited is leaving no stone unturned. RIL chairman Mukesh…
paragraph1: It’s already called the biggest IPO in India, but Reliance Industries Limited is leaving no stone unturned. RIL chairman Mukesh Ambani has reportedly urged all 4.2 Lakh Reliance employees to invest in the IPO, even paying their salaries in advance. Whether this is a show of strength or a safety net will only become clear after October 23 when the Jio Platforms IPO closes. RIL employees or not, investors will need to look at what can drive Jio’s growth from here and whether its digital businesses can deliver meaningful returns for those who back its IPO . The company’s ₹30,213 Cr IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with a price band of ₹1,065–₹1,119 per share. At the upper end, the issue values Jio Platforms at around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr. The offering comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, with the proceeds earmarked primarily for repaying certain borrowings of its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL). The breadth of the company is central to the investment case. Jio has spent years building a nationwide digital infrastructure and a large base of users who consume data, content and connected services. Jio Platforms reported revenue from operations of nearly ₹1.47 Lakh Cr in FY26, up from ₹1.28 Lakh Cr in FY25, while net profit rose to ₹30,049 Cr from ₹26,109 Cr. RJIL had 533.3 Mn customers as of June 30, 2026, and Jio’s network carried around 60% of India’s wireless data traffic in FY26, according to its RHP.
paragraph2: Its proposition, however, extends beyond mobile connectivity to fixed broadband, entertainment, cloud services, enterprise solutions and artificial intelligence (AI). But with most of the proceeds earmarked for debt repayment, it is imperative to examine how Jio Platforms makes money, whether its digital and AI ambitions can become meaningful growth engines, and what investors need to weigh against its scale and profitability. How Jio Platforms Makes Money Jio Platforms’ multifaceted business model rests on a simple premise: attract customers through connectivity and earn more from them through a range of digital services. The company operates through RJIL, its licensed telecom subsidiary, which provides mobile connectivity and fixed broadband. Other offerings span digital entertainment, gaming, cloud storage, smart-home solutions, enterprise connectivity and managed services. These include JioFiber, JioAirFiber, JioTV+, JioSaavn, JioAICloud, JioPC and JioBrain. For now, the financial trajectory remains closely linked to the underlying telecom business. Jio Platforms’ EBITDA rose 18.8% to ₹76,255 Cr in FY26, while the EBITDA margin expanded to 51.91% from 50.05% in FY25. “The margin improvement suggests that the company has been able to grow earnings faster than revenue, although investors will need to track how future network investments, depreciation and financing costs affect profitability,” an analyst at a leading brokerage firm said. The next question is how much more Jio can earn from its existing customer base. In the quarter ended June 2026, Jio’s average revenue per user (ARPU) rose 3.26% to ₹215.60 compared with ₹208.
paragraph3: 80 a year earlier. Monthly data consumption also increased to 43.7 GB per customer from 37 GB. These numbers point to a customer base that is using more data and generating more revenue per user. But rising consumption does not automatically translate into proportionate revenue growth. The company still needs to convert usage into higher-value plans, additional subscriptions and greater adoption of services beyond basic connectivity. RECOMMENDED FOR yOU Monetising Digital Services And AI Bets Jio’s digital-services narrative is built on the idea that its network, customer base and technology stack can support businesses beyond telecom. Its reach gives it a ready distribution channel: it can introduce digital products to millions of existing customers without having to acquire every user independently. The company’s fixed broadband business illustrates how it is extending that infrastructure into adjacent markets. Jio’s fixed broadband customer base grew from 11.2 Mn in March 2024 to 28.6 Mn in June 2026, including 14 Mn JioAirFiber customers. The fixed wireless access service uses its 5G infrastructure to connect homes without requiring a physical fibre connection to every premises, potentially making expansion faster in areas where laying fibre is difficult. The opportunity is significant because broadband can deepen household engagement beyond mobile data. JioHome combines connectivity with entertainment and smart-home services, while JioTV+ aggregates television channels and streaming services. JioAICloud offers cloud storage with AI-supported features, and JioPC provides cloud-based computing.
paragraph4: JioAICloud had approximately 66 Mn registered users as of June 30, 2026, according to the RHP. However, registered users are not the same as paying subscribers, and this is where the distinction between reach and monetisation becomes critical. A large user base can help a platform distribute new products, but the financial value depends on conversion rates, repeat usage, willingness to pay and the cost of delivering the service. The same scrutiny applies to Jio’s AI ambitions. The company says its proprietary AI engine, JioBrain, is embedded across network operations to support capacity allocation, fault prediction, resolution and real-time optimisation. It intends to extend these capabilities to other telecom operators and enterprise customers, alongside AI-powered customer services and automation tools. These ambitions could open up a different growth avenue. Rather than earning primarily from millions of individual mobile subscriptions, Jio could potentially sell technology, network-management capabilities and enterprise AI solutions to businesses. But this remains a proposition that is yet to prove. What Does Jio Platforms Offer Beyond Scale? Jio enters the public markets with a sizable customer base, expanding revenue and strong EBITDA margins. But the IPO valuation puts the spotlight on how much growth investors are already paying for. At the upper end of the ₹1,119 price band, Jio Platforms is valued at around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr. This gives the listing importance beyond the company itself: it will create a standalone market benchmark for a business that has so far been housed within Reliance Industries. Brokerage comparisons with Bharti Airtel underline the debate.
paragraph5: Nomura estimates Jio’s implied FY28 enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiple at around 10.5-10.9X, compared with 9.2X for Airtel’s India telecom business. The comparison also highlights the role of tariffs in future earnings. A price increase could lift ARPU across the sector, but the impact will depend on how customers respond, including whether they upgrade or downgrade plans, or leave the network. Jio’s wide customer base gives it reach, but its ability to translate higher prices into sustained revenue growth will depend on customer retention and the value it delivers. The one thing in Jio’s favour in this regard is that it has just Airtel as the competition at the top end. The two big players usually raise prices in unison which leaves little room for customer attrition. The IPO’s use of proceeds presents another important consideration. Jio Platforms plans to use up to ₹27,500 Cr of net proceeds to prepay, in full or in part, certain borrowings taken by RJIL, with the balance available for general corporate purposes subject to the offer-document conditions. This makes the issue partly a balance-sheet exercise. If it wasn’t clear already, this means investors should not treat the proceeds as funding that will automatically translate into new growth projects. The offering is also a fresh issue rather than an offer for sale, meaning the proceeds go to the company rather than existing shareholders selling down their holdings.

title: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
title_bn: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
author: TechPulse
excerpt: Benchmark may have grown its funds and swapped out some partners, but onstage the five who are left sounded like friends who just happen to be running one of the Valley’s most storied firms
paragraph1: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle. But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria. Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article. Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark? Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part. [As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye.
paragraph2: A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus. Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund? Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight. Ev, you’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ? Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn early to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team going out on the field together. And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other.
paragraph3: That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer. Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark? Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor.  .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn. I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda. Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.] Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday. Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light.
paragraph4: We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking. Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal. You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal? Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it. Altman: I actually don’t know. I was waiting to see what someone else did. It’s never happened? Altman: Because the firm is structured around a low volume of deals, you don’t actually want to have all of this rigor. If we invested in 100 or 200 companies a year, you’d want a CRM and a formal voting process. Because it’s so rare, the lack of structure is a huge asset. Fenton: One of the differentiating aspects of our brand is we’re not so cocksure to come in and say ‘winner’ or ‘loser.’ It’s not Shark Tank. We sort of feel awe, for lack of a better term, at all the possibilities .
paragraph5: . The occasional case where someone comes in who’s polarizing — the entrepreneurs feel that. If someone in the room doesn’t like you, we’re not a great partner. Companies are growing faster than ever. I’d think it’s easier to feel you’re missing out on opportunities if you don’t invest with greater frequency. Have you picked up the pace? Puttagunta: I think the pace is consistent. I think part of the reality of venture capital in our business is that we are not going to be part of every successful company, and that’s okay. There are companies that we identify, we find that the entrepreneur has some great strength, and we want to amplify that strength. And it’s our job to find a way to work with that person. It kind of doesn’t matter how much capital they want to raise, or what structure, or where they are. You just have to work through all that stuff. One thing that founders are interested in as a trend is VCs backing competing companies. Has that VC-founder pact changed because companies are growing so quickly and expanding into one another’s territory? Vishria: One of the things we have an ethos around is, we are making a commitment to an entrepreneur, and through that commitment, we’re saying we’re going to work with you in this thing, and whatever that thing is, and we are working closely enough where it matters, and it should matter to them, and as it matters to us.
